Alabama Pre-K tutorial: from the raw pipeline to reporting tables

Source: vignettes/alabama-tutorial.qmd 
library(catchmentACS)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)
library(tidyr)

# Force network-free, deterministic builds: no provider/Census calls, no cache.
old_options <- options(
  catchmentACS.progress = "off",
  catchmentACS.rate_first_default = FALSE
)
old_cache <- getOption("catchmentACS.cache_enabled", NULL)
on.exit(options(old_options), add = TRUE)
on.exit(options(catchmentACS.cache_enabled = old_cache), add = TRUE)
cacs_set_cache(FALSE, scope = "session")

This is the package’s long-form, flagship tutorial. Where vignette("getting-started", package = "catchmentACS") shows the whole pipeline in one call and vignette("methodology", package = "catchmentACS") explains the math, this article does two things in sequence. First it takes the one call apart — walking the five pipeline functions one stage at a time, reading each intermediate result, then collapsing them back into a single cacs_run() and confirming the two paths agree to the last digit. Then it carries the recomposed result all the way to the deliverables an equity researcher actually hands off: a site-by-drive-time rate matrix, a priority ranking, a single-site profile, and a tidy table ready to write to CSV.

It is written for a Pre-K equity researcher who wants to understand each stage well enough to describe it in a methods section, and who then needs to turn the output into a memo, a dissertation chapter, or a journal table. It assumes you have met dplyr, sf, isochrones, and margins of error before.

The motivating question comes from Pre-K funding-equity work: for each First Class Pre-K site, what are the neighborhood conditions — poverty, food assistance, employment — within a short drive, and how much do those conditions shift as the catchment grows from 5 to 15 minutes? catchmentACS is the reusable engine for that question. It replaces an earlier set of one-off analysis scripts with a documented, regression-tested package, so a finding can be reproduced — and a table re-generated — by a colleague who was not in the room when it was first run. Stable, uncertainty-aware answers feed directly into how the state reasons about where new Pre-K capacity should go.

About the data in this article

Every table, map, and figure here is built entirely from the package’s bundled inst/extdata fixtures (cacs_alabama_sites, the synthetic legacy_2025_* objects, and sample_alabama_subset), so this article renders with no Census, OSRM, ORS, or other network calls. These fixtures preserve the production calling contract (sites, drive-time polygons, tract-level ACS variables) but are synthetic and illustrative — included only for examples, tests, and reproducible package checks. They are not live Alabama policy estimates and must not be cited as real ACS results. Any real analysis requires a fresh live run (see vignette("providers", package = "catchmentACS")).

The data: Alabama Pre-K sites

A production run starts from a small table of program sites. The bundled cacs_alabama_sites shows the shape that table needs: a stable site identifier, a display name, a county FIPS code, a region label, and a single point geometry in EPSG:4326. These ten sites are the live-run template — coordinates are jittered and names are anonymized — so you can swap in your own administrative site list with the same columns and nothing else changes.

One bookkeeping note. cacs_alabama_sites is the live-run template; the executable path in this article instead uses the interlocking legacy_2025_* fixtures, because those carry the precomputed isochrones and the matching frozen baseline that let the whole document render offline and deterministically. So that the intermediate tables below stay small enough to read, the walkthrough uses three legacy sites — one northern, one north-central, one northwest — at drive times of 5, 10, and 15 minutes. The reasoning is identical for the full ten-site batch.

site_ids <- c("AL_SITE_03", "AL_SITE_07", "AL_SITE_08")

The pipeline, one stage at a time

cacs_run() orchestrates five functions in sequence. The first two reach the network; the last three are pure local computation on whatever those two returned:

cacs_acs_prefetch() (ACS download) → cacs_isochrone() (routing) → cacs_intersect_weight() → cacs_propagate_moe() → cacs_derive_rates().

This section runs each stage on its own so you can see the object that moves between them — and so you can lift any stage out as a standalone manuscript figure.

Stages 1 and 2 are network operations (shown, not run)

In a live run you would fetch statewide ACS tracts and draw drive-time isochrones like this. Both forms are shown for reference and are not executed here, because each would make a network request:

# Live form (needs a Census API key and network access):
acs <- cacs_acs_prefetch(state = "AL", year = 2023)
# Live form (needs a routing provider; the OSRM public demo needs no key):
iso <- cacs_isochrone(
  sites       = cacs_alabama_sites,
  drive_times = c(5, 10, 15),
  provider    = "osrm",
  osrm_mode   = "demo"
)

cacs_acs_prefetch() returns an sf tibble of tract-level ACS estimates (GEOID, NAME, variable, estimate, moe, geometry), and cacs_isochrone() returns one drive-time polygon per (site_id, drive_time_min) pair. The two bundled fixtures used below are exactly those return shapes, frozen: sample_alabama_subset.rds stands in for the ACS prefetch, and legacy_2025_isochrones.rds stands in for the isochrones. Loading them lets us run the rest of the pipeline with no network at all.

# These are exactly what stages 1 and 2 would have returned, frozen to disk.
sites <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "legacy_2025_sites.rds", package = "catchmentACS"
))
acs <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "sample_alabama_subset.rds", package = "catchmentACS"
))
iso <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "legacy_2025_isochrones.rds", package = "catchmentACS"
))

# Restrict to our three-site working batch and three drive-time bands.
analysis_sites <- sites |>
  filter(site_id %in% site_ids)
iso <- iso |>
  filter(site_id %in% site_ids, drive_time_min %in% c(5L, 10L, 15L))

list(
  acs_dim         = dim(acs),
  acs_crs         = sf::st_crs(acs)$epsg,
  acs_variables   = length(unique(acs$variable)),
  acs_tracts      = length(unique(acs$GEOID)),
  iso_dim         = dim(iso),
  iso_crs         = sf::st_crs(iso)$epsg
)
$acs_dim

$acs_crs
[1] 4269

$acs_variables
[1] 14

$acs_tracts
[1] 911

$iso_dim
[1]  9 16

The ACS fixture carries 14 source variables across the Alabama tracts in EPSG:4269; the isochrone fixture is a set of drive-time polygons in EPSG:4326. Those are the two coordinate systems cacs_intersect_weight() expects on input.

Stage 3: spatial intersection and area weighting

This is the algorithmic heart of the package. cacs_intersect_weight() overlays each isochrone on the ACS tracts, computes how much of each tract falls inside the catchment, and aggregates the source ACS counts by that overlap. It runs fully offline:

weighted <- cacs_intersect_weight(
  iso_sf        = iso,
  acs_sf        = acs,
  weight_method = "area",
  verbose       = FALSE
)

dim(weighted)
[1] 126  23
weighted |>
  select(site_id, drive_time_min, variable, estimate, weight_sum, n_tracts) |>
  arrange(site_id, drive_time_min, variable) |>
  head(8)
# A tibble: 8 × 6
  site_id    drive_time_min variable   estimate weight_sum n_tracts
  <chr>               <int> <chr>         <dbl>      <dbl>    <int>
1 AL_SITE_03              5 B01003_001       NA          1        1
2 AL_SITE_03              5 B11001_001     1625          1        1
3 AL_SITE_03              5 B17001_001     3896          1        1
4 AL_SITE_03              5 B17001_002     1016          1        1
5 AL_SITE_03              5 B19013_001    44119          1        1
6 AL_SITE_03              5 B19056_001     1322          1        1
7 AL_SITE_03              5 B19056_002      133          1        1
8 AL_SITE_03              5 B19301_001    22934          1        1

Two columns are worth reading closely. n_tracts is how many tracts the catchment touched — your sample thickness. weight_sum is the sum of the tract area weights that went into the aggregate; each weight is the fraction of a tract’s area lying inside the catchment, \text{coverage\_wt}_j = \text{area}(\text{catchment} \cap \text{tract}_j) / \text{area}(\text{tract}_j). Because catchments slice through tract boundaries, weight_sum is generally not a whole number — a catchment covering most of three tracts and the edge of a fourth might sum to something like 3.4. That is the answer to a reviewer who asks why the effective tract count is not an integer: tracts enter partially, in proportion to how much of their area the drive-time area covers.

The “Estimand families and weights” section of ?cacs_intersect_weight documents the full weighting scheme. In short, count variables (spatial_total) use this coverage weight directly, while scalar and proxy variables (a median-income proxy, say) use a separate normalized mean weight that sums to one within a cell. The function also attaches an internal carrier table — the coverage-weighted numerator and denominator totals — that the next two stages read.

Stage 4: margin-of-error propagation

ACS estimates ship with published margins of error (MOE), and those must travel through the weighting. cacs_propagate_moe() attaches an MOE to every row, choosing the formula appropriate to each variable’s estimand family. It is pure computation:

with_moe <- cacs_propagate_moe(weighted, verbose = FALSE)

with_moe |>
  select(site_id, drive_time_min, variable, estimate, moe,
         moe_formula_effective) |>
  arrange(site_id, drive_time_min, variable) |>
  head(8)
# A tibble: 8 × 6
  site_id    drive_time_min variable   estimate   moe moe_formula_effective
  <chr>               <int> <chr>         <dbl> <dbl> <chr>
1 AL_SITE_03              5 B01003_001       NA    NA weighted_sum
2 AL_SITE_03              5 B11001_001     1625   327 weighted_sum
3 AL_SITE_03              5 B17001_001     3896   599 weighted_sum
4 AL_SITE_03              5 B17001_002     1016   153 weighted_sum
5 AL_SITE_03              5 B19013_001    44119  9333 weighted_mean
6 AL_SITE_03              5 B19056_001     1322   225 weighted_sum
7 AL_SITE_03              5 B19056_002      133    27 weighted_sum
8 AL_SITE_03              5 B19301_001    22934  5685 weighted_mean

A margin of error is the half-width of a 90% confidence interval — you report a value as estimate ± moe, exactly as the Census Bureau reports ACS figures. This stage does not recompute the point estimates; it fills in moe and records, per row, which formula was used (moe_formula_effective) and whether any fallback was needed (moe_fallback, moe_fallback_reason). We do not re-derive those formulas here — the four families and the never-silent fallback rule are documented in ?cacs_propagate_moe and vignette("methodology", package = "catchmentACS").

One diagnostic habit: a non-trivial moe_fallback_reason is an audit signal, not an error. It records that a requested formula could not produce a value for a cell (for example a zero denominator or a missing input MOE) so the run stays transparent. In this intentionally clean mini-batch no fallback fires:

with_moe |>
  filter(moe_fallback_reason != "n/a" | failure_origin != "none") |>
  nrow()
[1] 0

Stage 5: derive the curated rates

Finally, cacs_derive_rates() appends the five curated catchment rates as new derived_rate rows beneath the source-variable rows, each as a ratio of area-weighted ACS totals with its own propagated MOE:

final <- suppressWarnings(cacs_derive_rates(with_moe, verbose = FALSE))

dim(final)
[1] 171  27
final |>
  filter(estimand_family == "derived_rate") |>
  select(site_id, drive_time_min, variable, estimate, moe,
         moe_formula_effective) |>
  arrange(site_id, drive_time_min, variable) |>
  head(10)
# A tibble: 10 × 6
   site_id    drive_time_min variable      estimate    moe moe_formula_effective
   <chr>               <int> <chr>            <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>
 1 AL_SITE_03              5 labor_force_…   0.323  0.0551 general_ratio_conser…
 2 AL_SITE_03              5 poverty_rate    0.261  0.0561 general_ratio_conser…
 3 AL_SITE_03              5 snap_rate       0.441  0.118  general_ratio_conser…
 4 AL_SITE_03              5 ssi_rate        0.101  0.0267 general_ratio_conser…
 5 AL_SITE_03              5 unemp_rate      0.0939 0.0238 general_ratio_conser…
 6 AL_SITE_03             10 labor_force_…   0.323  0.0551 general_ratio_conser…
 7 AL_SITE_03             10 poverty_rate    0.261  0.0561 general_ratio_conser…
 8 AL_SITE_03             10 snap_rate       0.441  0.118  general_ratio_conser…
 9 AL_SITE_03             10 ssi_rate        0.101  0.0267 general_ratio_conser…
10 AL_SITE_03             10 unemp_rate      0.0939 0.0238 general_ratio_conser…

Each rate maps to an ACS numerator/denominator pair and to a policy reading:

Rate ACS source Policy reading
poverty_rate B17001_002 / B17001_001 Catchment poverty — a demand-side proxy for Pre-K need
snap_rate B22003_002 / B22003_001 SNAP receipt — an administrative cross-check on household income stress
ssi_rate B19056_002 / B19056_001 Households with Supplemental Security Income — an equity dimension for disability/elderly-caregiver households
unemp_rate B23025_005 / B23025_003 Unemployment — parental labor-market attachment
labor_force_participation B23025_002 / B23025_001 Labor force participation — a supply-side (childcare-demand) proxy

The MOE formula for each rate is selected by cacs_derive_rates()’s formula_dispatch argument. Under the package’s baseline policy, poverty_rate and labor_force_participation are C1-eligible (the proportion_subset form, valid when the numerator is a true subset of the denominator), while snap_rate, ssi_rate, and unemp_rate are routed to C2 (general_ratio_conservative). A C1 rate whose subset variance comes out negative falls back to C2 for that cell, with the override recorded in moe_fallback, moe_fallback_reason, and moe_formula_effective. The full dispatch contract lives in ?cacs_propagate_moe and ?cacs_derive_rates.

Recompose into one call

The five stages above are exactly what cacs_run() does internally. Supplying both precomputed_isochrones = and acs = tells it to skip the two network stages and use the fixtures we loaded, so this one call reproduces the manual chain offline — no requests, no key:

result <- cacs_run(
  sites                  = analysis_sites,
  state                  = "AL",
  year                   = 2023,
  drive_times            = c(5, 10, 15),
  variables              = unname(cacs_acs_default_vars),
  provider               = "osrm",
  precomputed_isochrones = iso,
  acs                    = acs,
  weight_method          = "area",
  output                 = "long",
  verbose                = FALSE
)

class(result)
[1] "cacs_run_result" "tbl_df"          "tbl"             "data.frame"     
dim(result)
[1] 171  27

The provenance attribute confirms the path taken: both inputs were supplied, so the orchestrator ran the 3-call path (validation, intersection/weighting, MOE propagation, rate derivation, output assembly) with no network.

attr(result, "cacs_run_provenance") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(execution_path, provider, state, year,
         weight_method, formula_dispatch, bypass_iso, bypass_acs)
  execution_path provider state year weight_method           formula_dispatch
1         3-call     osrm    AL 2023          area general_ratio_conservative
2         3-call     osrm    AL 2023          area general_ratio_conservative
3         3-call     osrm    AL 2023          area general_ratio_conservative
  bypass_iso bypass_acs
1       TRUE       TRUE
2       TRUE       TRUE
3       TRUE       TRUE

And the result is identical to the hand-built chain — not merely close. Comparing the two estimate columns on the same (site_id, drive_time_min, variable) keys:

manual <- final |>
  arrange(site_id, drive_time_min, variable)
oneshot <- tibble::as_tibble(result) |>
  arrange(site_id, drive_time_min, variable)

c(
  same_nrow      = nrow(manual) == nrow(oneshot),
  max_estimate_d = max(abs(manual$estimate - oneshot$estimate), na.rm = TRUE),
  max_moe_d      = max(abs(manual$moe - oneshot$moe), na.rm = TRUE)
)
     same_nrow max_estimate_d      max_moe_d
             1              0              0

That zero is the point of the first half of this exercise: the readable five-stage decomposition and the single production call are the same computation. In daily work you write the one line; the five stages are what you cite in a methods section. The rest of the article works from result.

Reporting-ready outputs

This is the part that matters at hand-off. Everything below is a deliverable an equity researcher can drop into a memo, a dissertation chapter, or a journal submission — and each maps to a concrete reporting need.

Select the analyst-facing columns

result is one tidy long table — one row per site, drive-time band, and variable — carrying provenance and audit fields that are useful when you share results and ignorable otherwise. Most daily analysis starts from a handful of columns, so name them once and reuse the selection. Read failure_origin first: "none" is your success flag for that cell.

result_tbl <- tibble::as_tibble(result, rate_first = FALSE)

report_cols <- c(
  "site_id", "drive_time_min", "variable",
  "estimate", "moe", "n_tracts", "failure_origin"
)

result_tbl |>
  select(all_of(report_cols)) |>
  head(12)

This batch is intentionally clean, so every rate succeeds. In a larger live run, when a derived rate comes back NA, failure_origin names the stage that produced the gap — an upstream ACS input, an isochrone failure, an empty intersection, or a missing aggregation carrier — so you can diagnose rather than guess. The estimate for a rate is a proportion: 0.173 means 17.3%.

The site x drive-time rate matrix

The most compact deliverable is one row per site and drive time with all five curated rates side by side. Pivoting the long table wide gives exactly the shape of a manuscript table:

rate_matrix <- result_tbl |>
  filter(
    variable %in% names(cacs_acs_default_rates),
    failure_origin == "none"
  ) |>
  select(site_id, drive_time_min, variable, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = estimate) |>
  arrange(site_id, drive_time_min)

If a <NA> cell appears in a larger run, it is not a formatting error: it means the package could not form a stable numerator/denominator pair for that rate in that cell. Keep such cells visible in review tables rather than overwriting them with zero — a missing rate is a diagnostic, not an absence of need.

A 15-minute priority table

A common policy task is to rank sites by need at the widest catchment. Here we sort the three sites by their 15-minute poverty rate, highest first — the kind of ordering that drives a “where to invest next” conversation.

priority_15 <- result_tbl |>
  filter(
    drive_time_min == 15,
    variable == "poverty_rate",
    failure_origin == "none"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(estimate)) |>
  transmute(
    rank         = row_number(),
    site_id,
    poverty_rate = estimate,
    moe_90       = moe,
    n_tracts_num
  )

priority_15
# A tibble: 3 × 5
   rank site_id    poverty_rate moe_90 n_tracts_num
  <int> <chr>             <dbl>  <dbl>        <int>
1     1 AL_SITE_07        0.360 0.0472            3
2     2 AL_SITE_03        0.255 0.0351            3
3     3 AL_SITE_08        0.182 0.0296            3

The estimate stays a proportion; multiply by 100 only at the final formatting step so any downstream arithmetic remains stable. Swap poverty_rate for snap_rate or unemp_rate to rank on a different indicator, or change drive_time_min to compare priorities at a tighter band.

A focal-site profile

For a single-site memo the question is different: not “which site ranks highest?” but “how does this one site change as its catchment grows from 5 to 15 minutes?” The profile below shows all five curated rates across the three rings for one focal site, each with its margin of error and the implied confidence interval.

focal_site <- "AL_SITE_03"

result_tbl |>
  filter(
    site_id == focal_site,
    variable %in% names(cacs_acs_default_rates),
    failure_origin == "none"
  ) |>
  arrange(variable, drive_time_min) |>
  transmute(
    variable,
    drive_time_min,
    estimate,
    moe_90  = moe,
    ci_low  = pmax(estimate - moe, 0),
    ci_high = estimate + moe
  )

11 ssi_rate                              10   0.101  0.0267  0.0740  0.127

13 unemp_rate                             5   0.0939 0.0238  0.0701  0.118
14 unemp_rate                            10   0.0939 0.0238  0.0701  0.118
15 unemp_rate                            15   0.0664 0.00838 0.0580  0.0748

Reporting each rate as estimate ± moe_90 (or as the [ci_low, ci_high] interval shown here) is the same convention the Census Bureau uses for ACS figures, so a reviewer can read the catchment numbers exactly as they would read a published table.

An exportable report tibble

Finally, reduce the object to a clean, CSV-ready table. Keep the MOE, the failure flag, and the effective MOE formula alongside the estimate so a reviewer can trace both uncertainty and any fallback behavior.

export_tbl <- result_tbl |>
  filter(variable %in% names(cacs_acs_default_rates)) |>
  transmute(
    site_id,
    drive_time_min,
    variable,
    estimate,
    moe_90                = moe,
    estimate_pct          = 100 * estimate,
    moe_90_pct            = 100 * moe,
    failure_origin,
    moe_formula_effective,
    moe_fallback
  ) |>
  arrange(site_id, drive_time_min, variable)

head(export_tbl, 15)

You would write this out with, for example, readr::write_csv(export_tbl, "alabama_prek_rates.csv"). Before publishing any narrative claim, filter or flag rows where failure_origin != "none": a missing rate may still be a useful diagnostic, but it must not be read as zero.

Reproducibility and the frozen baseline

The package ships a frozen regression baseline, legacy_2025_golden_output.rds: the full ten-site, three-band cacs_run() result captured once and committed to inst/extdata. Its role is to anchor reproducibility — the test suite recomputes the pipeline and verifies it against this baseline at a tight numerical tolerance, so an accidental change in any stage’s arithmetic is caught before release.

golden <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "legacy_2025_golden_output.rds", package = "catchmentACS"
))

list(
  class          = class(golden)[1],
  dim            = dim(golden),
  n_sites        = length(unique(golden$site_id)),
  drive_times    = sort(unique(golden$drive_time_min))
)
$class
[1] "cacs_run_result"

$dim
[1] 1080   20

$n_sites
[1] 20

$drive_times
[1]  5 10 15

Its provenance records how it was produced — the same cacs_run() contract, captured on the 3-call (fixtures-only) path:

attr(golden, "cacs_run_provenance") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(execution_path, state, year, weight_method,
         formula_dispatch, output_format, level)
  execution_path state year weight_method           formula_dispatch
1         3-call    AL 2023          area general_ratio_conservative
2         3-call    AL 2023          area general_ratio_conservative
3         3-call    AL 2023          area general_ratio_conservative
  output_format level
1          long   0.9
2          long   0.9
3          long   0.9

What the guarantee means for you in practice: if you re-run the package on these bundled inputs and the recomputed estimates match the baseline within tolerance, your install reproduces the reference numbers exactly. That is the user-facing form of the regression check the maintainers run in CI — you can port a 2025-era analysis script onto this API and confirm the numbers did not move. A literal row-by-row comparison is only meaningful when it runs in a clean, offline-stable environment matching the one that produced the golden file (the same package version and spatial-library stack). The three-site batch above is a deliberately small slice for teaching, not the full-roster object the golden file records, so this article shows the baseline’s shape and provenance rather than asserting a numeric diff; the faithful comparison belongs in the test suite, which performs it at the locked tolerance.

A map

With the optional leaflet package installed, you can see one site’s 15-minute catchment over its intersecting tracts. This chunk is gated on the namespace, so it is simply skipped when leaflet is absent, and it calls leaflet:: rather than attaching the package.

# Focal site point and its 15-minute ring (both EPSG:4326).
focal_pt   <- analysis_sites[analysis_sites$site_id == focal_site, ]
focal_ring <- iso[iso$site_id == focal_site & iso$drive_time_min == 15, ]

# Build a tract-level poverty rate from the source ACS counts, then keep only
# the tracts the 15-minute ring touches. Everything stays offline.
suppressMessages(sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE))

pov <- acs |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(variable %in% c("B17001_001", "B17001_002")) |>
  select(GEOID, variable, estimate) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    id_cols = GEOID, names_from = variable, values_from = estimate
  ) |>
  transmute(GEOID, poverty_rate = B17001_002 / B17001_001)

tract_geom <- acs |>
  filter(variable == "B17001_001") |>
  select(GEOID) |>
  left_join(pov, by = "GEOID") |>
  sf::st_transform(4326)

hit <- tract_geom[
  sf::st_intersects(tract_geom, focal_ring, sparse = FALSE)[, 1],
]

pal <- leaflet::colorNumeric("YlOrRd", domain = hit$poverty_rate)

leaflet::leaflet(hit) |>
  leaflet::addProviderTiles("CartoDB.Positron") |>
  leaflet::addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(poverty_rate), fillOpacity = 0.6,
    weight = 0.5, color = "#666666",
    label = ~sprintf("Tract %s: %.1f%%", GEOID, 100 * poverty_rate)
  ) |>
  leaflet::addPolygons(
    data = focal_ring, fill = FALSE,
    weight = 2, opacity = 0.8, color = "#c05621"
  ) |>
  leaflet::addCircleMarkers(
    data = focal_pt, radius = 5, color = "#2b6cb0",
    fillOpacity = 0.9, stroke = FALSE, popup = ~site_id
  ) |>
  leaflet::addLegend(
    pal = pal, values = ~poverty_rate,
    title = "Tract poverty rate",
    labFormat = leaflet::labelFormat(transform = function(x) 100 * x, suffix = "%")
  )

The blue dot is the site, the orange outline is its 15-minute drive-time area, and the shaded tracts are everything that area touches, colored by tract poverty rate. This is the per-tract picture that area weighting collapses into a single catchment estimate. For a deeper map-based walkthrough, see vignette("visual-walkthrough", package = "catchmentACS").

Transition to a live run

To move from this offline walkthrough to current Alabama data, drop the two bypass arguments. The same cacs_run() call then draws drive-time areas from the selected provider and pulls ACS variables through tidycensus:

# One-time Census key setup:
tidycensus::census_api_key("YOUR_KEY_HERE", install = TRUE)

live_result <- cacs_run(
  sites         = cacs_alabama_sites,   # the 10 bundled sites, or your own roster
  state         = "AL",
  year          = 2023,
  drive_times   = c(5, 10, 15),
  variables     = unname(cacs_acs_default_vars),
  provider      = "osrm",
  weight_method = "area",
  output        = "long",
  verbose       = TRUE
)

A few notes for the live form:

  • Census key and ACS years. This release supports ACS 5-year end years 2009–2024 (2024 is the most recent vintage). A Census key is needed when the ACS request is a live cache miss or force_refresh = TRUE; a warm ACS cache hit, or supplying an explicit acs = object, needs no key.
  • Weighting. weight_method = "area" is the implemented method in this release. weight_method = "population" is a reserved name that fails loud at the orchestrator boundary before any network or spatial work begins — it is a planned future extension, not an active path.
  • Routing providers. "osrm" is implemented (the public demo endpoint needs no key but can be rate-limited), "ors" is implemented when the optional openrouteservice package and an API key are present, and "mapbox" and "r5r" are reserved fail-loud provider names.
